  ▎

  IV. The Letter

  The next morning a fishing boat came into the cove.
  Its captain was a tired man with salt in his beard.
  He climbed the rocks to thank her.

  "Saw your light just in time," he said. "Funny thing.
  My boy drowned out here twenty years ago. On nights
  like that I always feel like he's guiding me home."

  After he left, Mara finally opened the envelope.

  ▎ You've met him by now, I expect. He doesn't want
  ▎ anything except for his father to get home safe.
  ▎ His father is the last one who still fishes these
  ▎ waters. Keep the light until he stops coming. Then
  ▎ you can leave, and so can the boy.
  ▎
  ▎ — E.

  V. The Last Winter

  Mara stayed through that winter, and the next, and
  the one after that. She planted her seeds in the
  sheltered side of the rock, and they grew stubbornly
  in the salt air. Every foggy night she listened for
  the knocking, and she always answered it.

  In the fourth spring the old captain didn't come. A
  letter arrived instead: he had retired and moved
  inland to be near his sister.

  That night the fog rolled in. Mara waited at the
  bottom of the stairs until dawn, but nobody knocked.

  VI. For Whoever Comes Next

  Before she left, Mara wound the clockwork one last
  time and set a fresh envelope on the desk. On it she
  wrote For whoever comes next.

  Inside she put a packet of seeds and a single line:

  ▎ Answer the door. Someone is always trying to get
  ▎ home.

  ---

  The End.
